Ultrasound-diagnosed fatty liver in a Japanese health-check cohort

Dataset 9: Liver enzymes and arterial stiffness in a Japanese health-check cohort

RSR feasibility analysis

2026-08-03

Introduction

A general health-check programme in Japan enrolled 912 men and women aged 24 to 84 years and combined abdominal ultrasound, a fasting blood panel and automated vascular measurements in a single visit; the cohort is reported in BMJ Open 2014;4:e005413. Fatty liver was present on ultrasound in 265 (29.1%) of those scanned. Non-alcoholic fatty liver disease is now the commonest chronic liver condition in high-income countries and is a marker of insulin resistance as much as of liver injury, so knowing which routinely measured characteristics identify it at a health check is directly useful for triage.

Aim. Among these health-check attendees, we examined which of age, sex, body mass index, systolic blood pressure, smoking status, alcohol intake, regular exercise, fasting glucose, triglycerides, HDL cholesterol, kidney function and log2 gamma-GT are independently associated with ultrasound-diagnosed fatty liver, mutually adjusting for the others.

This is a Purpose 3 analysis: several predictors are of interest and the question is which remain associated with the outcome after mutual adjustment.

Methods

Data source. A cross-sectional Japanese health-check cohort of 912 adults attending a voluntary medical check-up programme that included abdominal ultrasound, a fasting blood panel and automated measurement of pulse-wave velocity and the ankle-brachial index.

Variables. The outcome is fatty_liver, a binary indicator where the event is fatty liver visible on abdominal ultrasound (265 events among the 911 participants scanned). Predictors are age (years), sex (reference Male, the larger group at 592 of 912), BMI (kg/m2), systolic blood pressure (mmHg), smoking status (three levels, reference Never, the largest group at 461), alcohol intake (g/week), regular exercise (reference No, the unexposed and larger group), fasting glucose (mg/dL), triglycerides (mg/dL), HDL cholesterol (mg/dL), estimated glomerular filtration rate (mL/min/1.73m2) and gamma-GT on a log2 scale, so that a one-unit increase is a doubling of GGT.

The predictor set was cut from 18 to 12 before any model was fitted. The events budget alone would not have forced this: with 253 events, the conventional ten-events-per-parameter rule supports about 25 parameters, and all 18 predictors would cost only 19. The cut was made instead for redundancy and interpretability. The suggested list contains three sets of near-duplicates. Systolic and diastolic pressure correlate at r = 0.90 (VIFs 5.1 and 5.3 with both in the model). The four lipid measures satisfy the Friedewald identity total = LDL + HDL + triglycerides/5 to within rounding: regressing total cholesterol on the other three gives R-squared 0.955 with coefficients 1.00, 1.06 and 0.17, and with all four in the model the VIFs reach 24.7 (total cholesterol) and 20.1 (LDL). ALT, AST and gamma-GT are the third set (ALT-AST r = 0.78). We therefore kept systolic pressure in place of both pressures; HDL cholesterol and triglycerides, the two metabolic-syndrome lipid components, in place of all four lipids; and log2 gamma-GT, the enzyme of interest in the source paper, in place of all three enzymes. Uric acid was dropped because it duplicates information already carried by adiposity and kidney function (r = -0.30 with eGFR, r = 0.38 with BMI). Beyond the statistics, a table of 18 mutually adjusted odds ratios cannot be read as an answer to “which predictors survive adjustment”, which is the question here.

Statistical analysis. glm(family = binomial), justified because the outcome is binary. We fitted a univariable model for each predictor first, then a single multivariable model containing all of them. Predictors were chosen in advance on subject-matter grounds, not by significance. Coefficients are exponentiated and reported as odds ratios with 95% confidence intervals; significance threshold 0.05. Model adequacy was assessed with performance::check_model(), focusing on binned residuals, collinearity, influential observations and events per parameter. Analysis used R version 4.6.0 (2026-04-24) with tidyverse, gtsummary and performance.

Missing data. Complete-case analysis: 882 of 912 rows were analysed (30 dropped), leaving 253 events. The outcome itself is missing for 1 participant; the rest of the loss is regular_exercise (16 missing) and alcohol_g_per_week (13 missing), which do not overlap. Only 844 of 912 rows are complete on every column in the file.

Participants with fatty liver are markedly heavier (median BMI 25.6 versus 22.1 kg/m2), have higher gamma-GT (median 4.58 versus 4.09 on the log2 scale, i.e. about 1.4-fold higher on the raw scale), higher fasting glucose and triglycerides and lower HDL cholesterol. They are overwhelmingly male (83% versus 58%), and their median age is essentially the same as the unaffected group, which is already a clue that this is a metabolic rather than a degenerative condition.

BMI is the strongest crude predictor by a wide margin: each additional kg/m2 multiplies the odds of fatty liver by OR 1.69 (95% CI 1.56 to 1.83) (p <0.001), which compounds to about 13.7-fold per 5 kg/m2. Each doubling of gamma-GT multiplies the odds by OR 2.11 (95% CI 1.76 to 2.54) (p <0.001). Women have OR 0.28 (95% CI 0.19 to 0.39) the odds of men (p <0.001), a nearly four-fold male excess. The metabolic panel behaves as expected: fasting glucose OR 1.08 (95% CI 1.06 to 1.09) per mg/dL (p <0.001), triglycerides OR 1.0106 (95% CI 1.0082 to 1.0132) per mg/dL (p <0.001, i.e. about 1.70-fold per 50 mg/dL), HDL cholesterol OR 0.94 (95% CI 0.92 to 0.95) per mg/dL (p <0.001), and systolic pressure OR 1.05 (95% CI 1.03 to 1.06) per mmHg (p <0.001). Regular exercise is associated with OR 0.46 (95% CI 0.30 to 0.69) (p <0.001), and both former (OR 1.50 (95% CI 1.07 to 2.12), p = 0.020) and current smoking (OR 1.61 (95% CI 1.11 to 2.33), p = 0.012) with raised odds. Two predictors show no crude association at all: age (OR 0.99 (95% CI 0.97 to 1.00), p = 0.120) and - strikingly, for a liver outcome - alcohol intake (OR 1.0002 (95% CI 0.9991 to 1.0013), p = 0.713).

Why adjustment is needed

Sex confounds the gamma-GT association hard. Men have roughly 1.5 times the GGT of women on the raw scale (medians 4.39 versus 3.81 on the log2 scale) and, independently of GGT, roughly four times the crude odds of fatty liver, so part of any apparent GGT effect is simply a male effect. BMI is the second, and it confounds nearly everything else in the list: heavier attendees have higher GGT (r = 0.28), higher triglycerides (r = 0.28), lower HDL (r = -0.31), higher blood pressure and higher glucose, and adiposity is the dominant cause of hepatic steatosis. Any crude lipid, pressure or enzyme association is therefore partly a body-mass association. Alcohol matters for the opposite reason. Drinking here is almost a proxy for being male (78% of men report any alcohol against 49% of women) and it is strongly associated with GGT (r = 0.33) and with triglycerides (r = 0.20). Being male and having high GGT both raise the odds of fatty liver sharply, so those two push the crude alcohol coefficient upward and cancel whatever the drinking itself is doing. Within men alone the pattern is already visible: 40% of male non-drinkers have fatty liver against 36% of male drinkers. Mutual adjustment lets each odds ratio be read as a comparison between attendees of the same age, sex, body mass, pressure, smoking, drinking, activity and metabolic profile.

The model has 253 events for 13 estimated parameters, i.e. 19.5 events per parameter, comfortably clear of the conventional minimum of ten. AIC falls from 1059.2 for the intercept-only model to 684.9, a drop of 374.3, and Tjur’s R-squared is 0.422 - a genuinely well-discriminating model by the standards of observational epidemiology.

Among attendees of the same age, sex, blood pressure, smoking, drinking, exercise, glucose, lipids, kidney function and gamma-GT, each additional kg/m2 of BMI multiplies the odds of fatty liver by OR 1.55 (95% CI 1.42 to 1.70) (p <0.001), about 9.0-fold per 5 kg/m2. Among attendees alike on everything else, each additional mg/dL of fasting glucose multiplies the odds by OR 1.05 (95% CI 1.03 to 1.08) (p <0.001) and each additional mg/dL of HDL cholesterol by OR 0.97 (95% CI 0.95 to 0.98) (p <0.001), i.e. about 0.71-fold per 10 mg/dL of HDL. Women retain OR 0.52 (95% CI 0.28 to 0.94) the odds of men (p = 0.032).

Two coefficients are worth dwelling on. Gamma-GT survives, but barely: each doubling gives OR 1.31 (95% CI 1.01 to 1.70) (p = 0.044), against a crude OR 2.11 (95% CI 1.76 to 2.54). Alcohol becomes protective: OR 0.9979 (95% CI 0.9963 to 0.9995) per g/week (p = 0.013), which compounds to about 0.81-fold per 100 g of weekly alcohol, having been exactly null in the crude model. Age (OR 0.99 (95% CI 0.97 to 1.02)), systolic pressure (OR 1.01 (95% CI 1.00 to 1.03)), triglycerides (OR 1.0017 (95% CI 0.9991 to 1.0044)), eGFR (OR 1.01 (95% CI 0.99 to 1.03)), regular exercise (OR 0.59 (95% CI 0.34 to 1.00)) and both smoking contrasts are not independently associated at the 0.05 level. These are associations among the attendees observed, not effects of intervening.

Gamma-GT moves furthest. It falls from OR 2.11 (95% CI 1.76 to 2.54) crude (p <0.001) to OR 1.31 (95% CI 1.01 to 1.70) adjusted (p = 0.044), which on the log-odds scale is about 64% of the way toward the null; the crude doubling-of-odds-per-doubling-of-GGT was mostly adiposity and sex. It only just clears 0.05 after adjustment, so the headline exposure of the source dataset is the most fragile coefficient in the model. Sex moves the same way, from OR 0.28 (95% CI 0.19 to 0.39) to OR 0.52 (95% CI 0.28 to 0.94) (p <0.001 to p = 0.032): roughly half of the crude four-fold male excess is explained by men being heavier, drinking more and having worse metabolic profiles, though a real excess remains. Triglycerides attenuate from OR 1.0106 (95% CI 1.0082 to 1.0132) to OR 1.0017 (95% CI 0.9991 to 1.0044) and lose significance entirely; so does systolic pressure (OR 1.05 (95% CI 1.03 to 1.06) to OR 1.01 (95% CI 1.00 to 1.03), p <0.001 to p = 0.056). Both were largely BMI.

Smoking reverses sign. Crude odds ratios were above one for both former (OR 1.50 (95% CI 1.07 to 2.12), p = 0.020) and current (OR 1.61 (95% CI 1.11 to 2.33), p = 0.012) smoking; adjusted they are below one and null (OR 0.70 (95% CI 0.42 to 1.16) and OR 0.80 (95% CI 0.46 to 1.37)). Smoking here is overwhelmingly a male behaviour - 17 of 320 women smoke currently, against 180 of 592 men - so the crude smoking association was a sex association. Alcohol goes the other way, from null to significant: OR 1.0002 (95% CI 0.9991 to 1.0013) crude (p = 0.713) to OR 0.9979 (95% CI 0.9963 to 0.9995) adjusted (p = 0.013). This is classic masking, and it can be traced variable by variable: adding sex alone to the crude alcohol model moves the log-odds coefficient from 0.20 to -1.07 per 1,000 g/week, and adding log2 gamma-GT alone moves it to -1.77. Drinkers are male and have high GGT, and both of those raise the odds of fatty liver; holding them constant unmasks a negative residual association.

Two barely move. BMI goes from OR 1.69 (95% CI 1.56 to 1.83) to OR 1.55 (95% CI 1.42 to 1.70) and fasting glucose from OR 1.08 (95% CI 1.06 to 1.09) to OR 1.05 (95% CI 1.03 to 1.08) - modest attenuation in both cases, but they remain the two strongest predictors in the model and are not explained away by anything else measured here.

Diagnostics

## Warning: Probably bad model fit. Only about 70% of the residuals are inside the error bounds.

Binned residuals are the check that fails. Only 70% of binned residuals lie inside their error bounds, against a target of 95% or more, so the model is measurably miscalibrated somewhere across the fitted-probability range. With 253 events spread over 882 observations each bin holds around 29 participants, so the check is noisy, but the pattern is consistent with the linear-in-log-odds assumption failing for BMI: the BMI-steatosis relationship is steeper in the middle of the range than at either extreme, and a single linear term cannot capture that.

Collinearity is not a problem in the reduced model. The largest VIF is 1.56 (sex), well below the conventional threshold of 5. In the 18-predictor version the largest VIF is 24.7, so the a-priori cut is doing real work.

There is no separation. All coefficients are finite, the largest standard error on the log-odds scale is 0.31, and every level of every categorical predictor contains events (the smallest cell is 1 - female current smokers with fatty liver - which is thin but not empty). That cell is worth noting because it is where a student adding a sex * smoking_status interaction would run into trouble: with 16 female current smokers in total, the interaction contrast is estimated from almost nothing and its standard error explodes.

Influence is unremarkable. The largest Cook’s distance is 0.098 and the largest leverage 0.383; no single participant drives the fit.

Homogeneity of variance and normality of residuals do not apply to a logistic model and are not interpreted; the corresponding panels of check_model() should be ignored here.

Finally, a targeted check of the liver-enzyme decision. Adding ALT and AST back alongside gamma-GT does not produce alarming VIFs (largest 2.24), but it reverses the sign of the gamma-GT coefficient: GGT goes from OR 1.31 (95% CI 1.01 to 1.70) in the model above to OR 0.64 (95% CI 0.45 to 0.89) (p = 0.010) with the other two enzymes present, while ALT takes over as the enzyme of record (OR 1.09 (95% CI 1.06 to 1.13) per U/L, p <0.001). Three correlated markers of the same organ competing for the same variance is exactly the situation in which a conditional coefficient stops meaning what its name suggests, and it is the main reason only one enzyme is carried in the primary model.

Discussion

In this Japanese health-check cohort, ultrasound fatty liver is above all a metabolic condition: body mass index and fasting glucose are the two dominant independent predictors, with each 5 kg/m2 of BMI multiplying the odds by about 9.0 and each 10 mg/dL of HDL cholesterol dividing them by about 1.41, holding everything else constant. Gamma-GT, the marker this cohort was assembled to study, retains a small independent association (OR 1.31 (95% CI 1.01 to 1.70) per doubling) that only just reaches significance, and roughly three-quarters of its crude association is explained by adiposity and sex. Alcohol intake is inversely associated with fatty liver once body mass and GGT are held constant, which is a reminder that ultrasound steatosis in a screening population is largely non-alcoholic. In practice, BMI and a fasting glucose identify most of the risk; the liver enzymes add little beyond them.

Limitations. The design is cross-sectional, so temporal order is unknown and reverse causation is entirely plausible - a fatty liver raises GGT, so the GGT-steatosis association almost certainly runs partly backwards from outcome to “predictor”. The outcome is ultrasound-defined, which is operator-dependent, has limited sensitivity for mild steatosis and is degraded by obesity itself, so misclassification is probably differential with respect to BMI, the strongest predictor. Health-check attendees are self-selected and healthier than the general Japanese population, which compresses the range of every risk factor and will attenuate the odds ratios. Alcohol is self-reported in g/week with 284 attendees reporting exactly zero, and under-reporting by heavy drinkers is the standard failure mode - the protective alcohol coefficient should not be read as evidence that drinking prevents fatty liver. No medication data are available, so statins, antihypertensives and glucose-lowering drugs are unmeasured confounders. Waist circumference, insulin, HOMA-IR and viral hepatitis status are absent, and the first two are more direct measures of the visceral adiposity and insulin resistance that drive this condition than BMI is. The binned-residual check fails (70% inside bounds), indicating miscalibration that a non-linear term for BMI would probably improve. Complete-case analysis dropped 30 of 912 rows. All estimates are associations, not causal effects.

Future work. Refit with a spline or fractional polynomial for BMI to address the calibration failure, and add waist circumference and a fasting insulin measure so that the model separates visceral adiposity from body mass.

Feasibility notes

NOT part of a student report.

  • Verdict: USABLE. This is the strongest of the four outcomes in this dataset. 253 events on 882 complete cases, 19.5 events per parameter, Tjur’s R-squared 0.422, no separation, no collinearity problem and a clear, real signal. A competent student will get a clean model.
  • MAJOR: binned residuals fail - only 70% of bins inside the error bounds against a 95% target. This is genuine miscalibration (the BMI-steatosis relationship is not linear in the log odds) rather than pure noise, and an honest student has to report a failed check. It is a good teaching case, but it will unsettle students who expect diagnostics to pass.
  • MAJOR: three correlated liver enzymes, and the choice between them changes the sign of the answer. With only log2_ggt in the model, GGT is OR 1.31 (95% CI 1.01 to 1.70) (p = 0.044). Add alt and ast and GGT becomes OR 0.64 (95% CI 0.45 to 0.89) (p = 0.010) - a protective association - while ALT becomes the dominant enzyme (OR 1.09 (95% CI 1.06 to 1.13), p <0.001). The VIFs never exceed 2.2, so nothing warns the student that this has happened. This is the single most likely way a student produces a confidently wrong conclusion from this outcome, and it belongs in the meta.json cautions.
  • MAJOR collinearity if all four lipids are used. VIFs in the 18-predictor logistic model: 24.7 (total cholesterol), 20.1 (LDL), 4.4 (HDL), 5.7 (triglycerides). Regressing total cholesterol on the other three gives R-squared 0.955 with coefficients 1.00 / 1.06 / 0.17, i.e. the Friedewald identity. It is near-deterministic, not exact - the residual total_cholesterol - hdl_cholesterol - triglycerides/5 - ldl_cholesterol has a median of about 8.0 mg/dL - so the model fits without complaint and simply becomes uninterpretable.
  • MAJOR collinearity between the blood pressures (r = 0.90; VIFs 5.1 and 5.3 with both in).
  • MAJOR: the exposure of interest is plausibly downstream of the outcome. A steatotic liver leaks enzymes; GGT rises because of fatty liver at least as much as the reverse. Every GGT-fatty-liver statement in a cross-sectional file is uninterpretable causally, and the “predictor” framing invites students to get this backwards.
  • MINOR: near-separation risk only via interactions. No main-effect term separates. The thinnest cell is 1 (female current smokers with fatty liver, out of 16 female current smokers). A sex * smoking_status interaction is therefore estimated from almost nothing; the coefficients stay finite but the standard errors are useless. Smoking is 91% male in this file.
  • MINOR: alcohol flips from exactly null to significantly protective on adjustment (OR 1.0002 (95% CI 0.9991 to 1.0013) to OR 0.9979 (95% CI 0.9963 to 0.9995)). Correct arithmetic, dangerous prose - a weak student will write that alcohol protects the liver. The mechanism is masking by BMI and sex, and the real explanation is under-reporting plus the fact that ultrasound steatosis here is mostly non-alcoholic.
  • MINOR: complete-case loss is small - 882 of 912 (3.3%), from regular_exercise (16 missing), alcohol_g_per_week (13 missing) and one missing outcome. Events fall from 265 to 253, which changes nothing.
  • MINOR: no medication, waist circumference, insulin or hepatitis serology. Residual confounding is certain, and BMI is a blunt proxy for the visceral adiposity that actually drives steatosis.
  • The outcome is not a deterministic function of any shipped column: the best single-variable discrimination is BMI, and even a BMI-only model reaches Tjur’s R-squared only 0.30.
